newsitem.title: GERMANY: More Euro-mergers to trample bank-insurer fence.
newsitem.headline: More Euro-mergers to trample bank-insurer fence.

text.p: This week's shock merger between Credit Suisse and Winterthur will not be the last as Europe's financial services industry tramples the fence between banks and insurers.
"We expect this merger trend to continue unabated into the foreseeable future," said Mark Hoge, European banking analyst at CS First Boston in London.

The spur is two-fold. In an era when pension provision is falling firmly into private hands, a bank-insurer merger can capitalise on a larger customer base and pooled expertise to gain a share of the lucrative investment management market.
Secondly, banks and insurers can target each other's customers, offering home insurance to new mortgage customers, or savings accounts to those with life insurance for example.

For many analysts, the brightest spotlight falls on Germany -- most recently scene of a bank merger in Bavaria -- where takeover rumours have propelled shares in financial services firms to unprecedented highs.
Hoge sees Commerzbank AG, Germany's third-largest private sector bank, as a prime takeover candidate.
"The clearest combinations in Europe are in Germany. Our basic view is that Commerzbank will not be here a year from now."
Mergers and acquisitions have become commonplace in European financial services, where liberalisation has raised the competitive stakes and where economies of scale are essential for survival.

But big-ticket deals like the merger announced on Monday between Swiss bank Credit Suisse Group and insurer Winterthur Group still carry a shock value, underlining that "bancassurance" (a hybrid of banking and insurance) may be the way forward.
Such huge fusions remain relatively rare, with ING of the Netherlands being Europe's only true exponent of a fully merged banking-cum-insurance company.

The new Swiss group will be one of the world's 10 biggest financial services companies with a stock market capitalisation of some $37 billion, and the world's third largest asset manager for private and institutional investors, with $465 billion under management.

"When we look ahead, it is clear that there will not be a banking industry and an insurance industry in Europe, but a financial services industry," said Ian McEwen, banking analyst at Lehman Brothers in London.
McEwen is sceptical on the strategic significance of the CS/Winterthur deal, arguing that the motive for the deal was to raise capital rather than to achieve synergies.
The most interesting point about this merger is what the new group -- armed with its increased buying power -- will acquire next, he said.
McEwen and other analysts see more mergers and acquisitions between banks and insurance companies as likely to occur all over Europe.
French financial services are undergoing a major overhaul as the government gears up to sell off ailing banking giant Credit Lyonnais and insurer GAN.
Movement may be afoot in the Netherlands, where both ABN AMRO and ING are thought to be on a buying trail.
But Germany could provide the hottest news.
This year has seen a series of moves which have rocked an industry long dominated by Deutsche Bank AG, which has extensive insurance operations, and Allianz AG, the Munich-based insurer.

The biggest by far was last month's news of plans to merge Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG to create a Bavarian bank of which Allianz will own about 16 percent.

The deal raises several questions -- what will Deutsche, which had a strategic interest in Vereinsbank, do to level the field with its ancient rival Allianz and what will Dresdner Bank AG, which will be deposed by the newcomer as the Number 2 in German banking, do to beef up its position?
Most pressing of all is the question as to what Commerzbank -- a relative minnow compared with Deutsche and Allianz -- can do to survive in a fast consolidating market.
Analysts have dozens of plausible theories on the most likely next move in German financial services.
One is that Allianz and Dresdner Bank, already linked though cross-shareholdings and close partners on a distribution level, could intensify their co-operation or merge.

A second is that Deutsche or Dresdner will buy Commerzbank, although that will prove problematic in this consensus-based culture unless Commerzbank drops its opposition to a takeover. A third theory, and the most potent as regards stock market exuberance, is that Commerzbank will be bought up from abroad, possibly by a Swiss bank.
"As an investment bet, I'd go for Commerzbank being bought up, and soon," said CS First Boston's Hoge.

A foreign buy-out of Commerzbank would finally satisfy years of market speculation that such a move was imminent, but it is a moot point as to how viable cross-border financial services in Europe can be.
Differing tax situations and investment habits make the creation of a standard "Euro-product", especially in boom areas like wealth management, a difficult proposition.
"People talk about one huge cross-border financial conglomerate in Europe or a Europe dominated by a handful of names. I would be a sceptic," said Lehman Brothers McEwen.
"I think this sector will remain essentially fragmented."
